description:
The red imported fire ant is a small, aggressive ant, 2 to 6 mm long, with a reddish-brown body and a darker abdomen. It builds loose, dome-shaped dirt mounds in open, disturbed ground - lawns, parks, footpaths, schoolyards and garden beds. Unlike native Australian ants it has no natural predators here, so colonies grow quickly and each queen can lay thousands of eggs.

Every colony defends its mound ferociously. When the nest is disturbed, hundreds of workers swarm out and sting repeatedly, each ant able to sting several times. The sting feels like a sharp burn and leaves a white pustule that can last weeks; a small number of people have a severe allergic reaction. The ants also damage electrical equipment, crops and native wildlife.

Fire ants were first detected in Queensland in 2001 and are under an official national eradication program. If you find a mound, do not disturb it - mark the spot from a distance, keep pets and children away, and report it immediately so a trained team can treat it.
typicalHabitat: Open, disturbed ground: lawns, playing fields, roadsides, garden mulch and along footpaths
sizeRange: Workers 2-6 mm; queens up to 9 mm
disposalGuidance: Do not disturb the mound - disturbed ants scatter and start new colonies. Keep children and pets away, mark the spot, and report it to the National Fire Ant Eradication Program. Do not attempt to treat the nest yourself; eradication teams apply the registered bait.
reportAuthority: National Fire Ant Eradication Program - biosecurity.qld.gov.au

description:
The cane toad is a large, warty amphibian, typically 10 to 15 cm long, with dry, leathery brown skin, a pale belly and distinctive parotoid glands bulging behind each eye. It was brought to Queensland from Hawaii in 1935 in a failed attempt to control cane beetles, and has since spread across much of northern and eastern Australia.

The toad's shoulders carry a milky poison called bufotoxin. When threatened it squeezes the poison out; this toxin can kill native predators such as goannas, quolls and snakes that try to eat it, and it can make pets very sick if they bite or lick a toad. Cane toads breed in almost any still water, lay long strings of 30,000 or more eggs, and can live for several years.

Cane toads are widespread in Brisbane. They gather around outdoor lights at night hunting insects, and shelter in gardens, drains and under buildings during the day.
typicalHabitat: Moist gardens, drains, under buildings, and around outdoor lights and water features
disposalGuidance: Never squeeze or handle a cane toad bare-handed - the shoulder toxin can irritate skin and can kill pets that mouth the toad. Report sightings to Biosecurity Queensland and ask about a collection or control program in your area before acting. If removal is permitted where you live, wear gloves and follow the humane method approved by your council.

description:
Water hyacinth is a free-floating aquatic plant with glossy, rounded leaves and striking mauve flowers on tall stalks. Each plant is buoyed by spongy, air-filled stems, which lets it drift and form thick mats on the surface of dams, ponds, canals and slow rivers.

The mats are the problem: they block out sunlight, strip oxygen from the water as they rot, smother native water plants and make boating and fishing impossible. One plant can multiply quickly - under good conditions a single mat can double in size in less than two weeks - so a small clump dumped in a waterway becomes a whole dam's worth of weed within a season.

Water hyacinth is a declared weed of national significance in Australia. It rarely sets seed in this country, which is good news: because it spreads mostly by fragments, preventing people from dumping plant material into waterways is the single most effective control.
typicalHabitat: Still or slow freshwater: dams, ponds, canals, stormwater basins and river backwaters
sizeRange: Plants 10-30 cm high; flowers 3-8 cm across
disposalGuidance: Never dump aquarium or pond plants into waterways, drains or compost where fragments can wash away. Report waterway infestations to your council or Biosecurity Queensland. Removal must take every leaf and root fragment out of the water, or the weed grows back from what is left.

description:
The Asian house gecko is a small, slender lizard, 10 to 13 cm long including its tail, with a grey to pinkish-brown body, lighter belly and rows of tiny tubercles on its back. It is nocturnal and almost always found around buildings, hunting insects on walls and ceilings where lights attract moths.

House geckos arrived in Australia as stowaways in cargo and are now common in homes and sheds across northern Australia, including Brisbane. They are completely harmless to people - they cannot bite through skin and carry no venom. Their main nuisance value is the loud, chirping call males make at night and the droppings they leave behind lights.

In their native Asia these geckos live in trees and rock crevices; in Australia they have simply swapped cliffs for brick walls. They are established here but are not considered a significant pest.
typicalHabitat: Warm buildings, sheds, patios and tree trunks near artificial light
disposalGuidance: No action needed - house geckos are harmless and eat insects. To discourage them indoors, seal gaps around doors and windows, reduce outdoor lights that attract moths, and never use sticky or glue traps. If one gets inside, guide it into a container and release it outside near shelter.
reportAuthority: Introduced but not a declared pest - no reporting required

description:
The common (or Indian) myna is a chunky, chocolate-brown bird about 23 to 26 cm long with a black head, yellow beak, yellow eye-patch and white wing flashes that are obvious in flight. It walks rather than hops and is usually seen in pairs or small groups on lawns, in car parks and around outdoor cafe tables.

Mynas are aggressive cavity-nesters. They evict native birds such as rosellas and kookaburras from tree hollows and roof cavities, and they crowd out smaller birds from feeding areas. They are at their most numerous in suburbs, where lawns, pet food and open rubbish give them everything they need to breed several times a year.

Native to southern Asia, mynas arrived in Australia in the 1800s and are now one of the most successful urban birds in the country. They are not a declared pest in Queensland, but their impact on native birds has led many councils to run trapping and removal programs.
conservationStatus: Not listed - impact on native birds
typicalHabitat: Suburban and urban areas: lawns, parks, car parks, rooflines and tree hollows
disposalGuidance: Do not harm or relocate mynas yourself. Remove the food sources that feed them - uncovered pet food, seed on the ground and accessible rubbish. If mynas are nesting in roof cavities, block entry points after the chicks have fledged. Ask your local council whether a trapping program operates in your area.
reportAuthority: Local council - not a declared pest in Queensland

description:
The red fox is a dog-sized predator, 60 to 75 cm of body with a thick, bushy tail, rusty-red fur, white chest and black-tipped ears and legs. In cities it is mostly seen at dawn and dusk, slipping along fence lines, through bushland edges and across parklands.

Foxes were introduced to Australia in the 1800s for hunting and are now found across most of the continent. They are opportunistic hunters and scavengers, taking ground-nesting birds, lizards, small mammals and lambs, and they raid bins for food scraps. Around Brisbane they breed in dens dug into hillsides and under sheds, producing four to six cubs a year.

Foxes can carry diseases that affect pets and people, including hydatid tapeworm and sarcoptic mange. They are a declared pest in Queensland, which means landholders and councils have a legal obligation to keep numbers down and report established populations.
typicalHabitat: Bushland edges, farmland, parklands and the rural-urban fringe, denning in earth burrows
disposalGuidance: Do not approach or feed foxes - they can carry diseases and may bite if cornered. Secure bins and remove pet food so foxes are not attracted to your yard. Report foxes denning on your property, stock losses or sick animals to Biosecurity Queensland; baiting and shooting are regulated and usually run by councils or coordinated landcare groups.

description:
Lantana is a scrambling, prickly shrub that grows 1 to 4 m tall, with rough, pungent leaves and dense clusters of small flowers that change colour from yellow to orange to red as they age. It forms impenetrable thickets along forest edges, roadsides and cleared pastures.

The thickets crowd out native grasses and seedlings, block fences and walking tracks, and shelter feral pigs and foxes. The leaves and unripe berries are toxic to livestock, and the plant's ability to regrow from any stem or root fragment makes it one of Australia's worst environmental weeds. It burns readily, which makes infestations a fire hazard near homes.

Lantana is a weed of national significance, and in Queensland it is a restricted invasive plant in several areas. Birds spread the seeds into new bushland, so control often works best by tackling the oldest, largest patches first and following up so regrowth does not reseed.
typicalHabitat: Forest edges, roadsides, creek lines and cleared or grazed land
disposalGuidance: Wear gloves, long sleeves and eye protection - the stems are prickly and the foliage can irritate skin. Hand-pull or scrape small plants, removing the root crown; for large thickets call a licensed contractor. Do not burn freshly pulled plants, as heat can trigger seeds on the ground, and do not dump material where it can regrow.

description:
The green tree frog is a large, plump frog, 7 to 10 cm long, bright green above and white below, with cream or gold stripes down its sides and large toe pads that let it cling to glass and leaves. In Brisbane it is the frog people most often find in their homes - in showers, toilets, pot plants and around veranda lights.

This is a native Australian species and a very useful one: a single adult eats thousands of insects, mosquitoes and moths a year. It is most active on warm, wet nights, calling with a deep, almost dog-like sound that carries across gardens. It breeds in any plentiful water source, from permanent ponds to a bucket left out in the rain.

Because it is native, the green tree frog is protected. It is not a pest, and it should not be confused with the cane toad, which is larger, warty all over, and never climbs glass with round toe pads. Finding one on your property is a sign of a healthy garden.
typicalHabitat: Trees and buildings near water; garden ponds, rain gutters and sheltered corners
disposalGuidance: Native and protected - enjoy it and leave it in place. Frogs often investigate houses after rain; if one is indoors, guide it into a container and release it gently into garden cover at dusk. Keep pools and tanks covered so frogs do not drown, and avoid garden chemicals that wash into their breeding water.
reportAuthority: Native protected species - no reporting required

description:
The striped marsh frog is a medium-sized ground frog, 5 to 7 cm long, brown or grey with four dark stripes running down its back and a pale, mottled belly. It is one of the most common frogs in south-east Queensland and is frequently seen around ponds, flooded lawns and backyard wetlands after rain.

Females are noticeably larger than males. In spring the males chorus from floating grass at the water's edge, calling with a short, repetitive note that can sound almost like a dripping tap. The species breeds opportunistically - any substantial rain can trigger spawning in temporary pools, puddles and dams.

Like the green tree frog, the striped marsh frog is native to eastern Australia. It is not a pest and is harmless to people and gardens. Its presence means there is clean water and insect life nearby, and it helps keep mosquito numbers down in the warmer months.
typicalHabitat: Ponds, wetlands, dams and flooded grass; lawns after heavy rain
disposalGuidance: Native - leave it in place and protect backyard wetlands. Avoid draining ponds during the breeding season, keep garden chemicals out of waterways, and never release pets or exotic animals into frog habitat. Reporting is not required for native species.
reportAuthority: Native protected species - no reporting required

description:
The noisy miner is a grey-backed honeyeater about 23 to 28 cm long with a black crown and face, a yellow bill and a distinctive yellow patch behind each eye. It is one of Australia's most common urban birds, usually seen in small flocks foraging on lawns and in tree canopies and calling constantly.

Despite the similar name, noisy miners are not related to the introduced common myna. They are native to eastern Australia. Their impact comes from their mobbing behaviour: groups aggressively chase away almost every other bird from their territory - honeyeaters, wrens, finches and even much larger birds like kookaburras - which can leave local woodlands dominated by miners and little else.

Miners thrive in open, well-mown parks and gardens because those habitats suit them and disadvantage the small birds they displace. They are a native species, not a declared pest, and they also do important work controlling insects - their numbers simply need balance, and the best lever is habitat rather than removal.
typicalHabitat: Open woodland, parklands and suburban gardens with large trees and short grass
disposalGuidance: Native - no removal is needed and it is not legal to harm them. To reduce their dominance in your garden, plant dense, layered native understorey and shrubs, which give smaller birds somewhere to hide and feed, and reduce lawn area so the habitat is less miner-friendly.
